claim: Cancer patients often harbor occult metastases, a potential source of relapse that is targetable only through systemic therapy.
source: Cancer patients often harbor occult metastases, a potential source of relapse that is targetable only through systemic therapy.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Studies of occult metastases have been limited by a lack of tools with which to isolate discrete cells on spatial grounds.
source: Studies of this occult fraction have been limited by a lack of tools with which to isolate discrete cells on spatial grounds.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of the field and is supported by the context of existing methodological limitations.

claim: PIC-IT is a photoconversion-based isolation technique allowing efficient recovery of cell clusters of any size.
source: We developed PIC-IT, a photoconversion-based isolation technique allowing efficient recovery of cell clusters of any size – including single-metastatic cells – which are largely inaccessible otherwise.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript demonstrating the technique's capabilities.

claim: PIC-IT enables recovery of single-metastatic cells which are largely inaccessible otherwise.
source: We developed PIC-IT, a photoconversion-based isolation technique allowing efficient recovery of cell clusters of any size – including single-metastatic cells – which are largely inaccessible otherwise.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing isolation of microcolonies of 1-10 cells.

claim: Transcriptional profiling of spontaneously arising microcolonies in a murine pancreatic cancer model revealed phenotypic heterogeneity.
source: In a murine pancreatic cancer model, transcriptional profiling of spontaneously arising microcolonies revealed phenotypic heterogeneity, functionally reduced propensity to proliferate and enrichment for an inflammatory-response phenotype associated with NF-κB/AP-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and UMAP clustering analysis showing multiple distinct clusters.

claim: Microcolonies have functionally reduced propensity to proliferate compared to macrometastases.
source: In a murine pancreatic cancer model, transcriptional profiling of spontaneously arising microcolonies revealed phenotypic heterogeneity, functionally reduced propensity to proliferate and enrichment for an inflammatory-response phenotype associated with NF-κB/AP-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo proliferation assays, immunostaining for cell cycle markers, and transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Microcolonies show enrichment for an inflammatory-response phenotype associated with NF-κB/AP-1 signaling.
source: In a murine pancreatic cancer model, transcriptional profiling of spontaneously arising microcolonies revealed phenotypic heterogeneity, functionally reduced propensity to proliferate and enrichment for an inflammatory-response phenotype associated with NF-κB/AP-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing enrichment of TNF-α-NF-κB signaling genes, motif analysis, and immunostaining for NF-κB-p65 and phospho-c-Jun.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB depleted microcolonies but had no effect on macrometastases.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB depleted microcolonies but had no effect on macrometastases, suggesting microcolonies are particularly dependent on this pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from triptolide treatment experiments showing differential effects on microcolonies versus macrometastases.

claim: Microcolonies are particularly dependent on the NF-κB pathway.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB depleted microcolonies but had no effect on macrometastases, suggesting microcolonies are particularly dependent on this pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential response to NF-κB inhibition between microcolonies and macrometastases.

claim: Metastasis is the primary cause of cancer-associated mortality.
source: Metastasis is the primary cause of cancer-associated mortality and remains a significant therapeutic challenge.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: Metastasis remains a significant therapeutic challenge.
source: Metastasis is the primary cause of cancer-associated mortality and remains a significant therapeutic challenge.
evidence: This reflects the current state of cancer treatment and is widely accepted in the field.

claim: A considerable fraction of metastasis is occult.
source: A considerable fraction of metastasis is occult (Haeno et al., 2012; Vanharanta and Massagué, 2013) and thus serves a potential source for residual disease and recurrence (Sosa et al., 2014; Tohme et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Occult metastasis serves as a potential source for residual disease and recurrence.
source: A considerable fraction of metastasis is occult (Haeno et al., 2012; Vanharanta and Massagué, 2013) and thus serves a potential source for residual disease and recurrence (Sosa et al., 2014; Tohme et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fluorescent reporters allow detection of metastatic colonies in pre-clinical models.
source: While fluorescent reporters allow detection of metastatic colonies in pre-clinical models (Aiello et al., 2016; Fluegen et al., 2017), an inability to recover pure micron-scale colonies has precluded systematic phenotypic analysis of early-stage metastases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using fluorescent reporters.

claim: An inability to recover pure micron-scale colonies has precluded systematic phenotypic analysis of early-stage metastases.
source: While fluorescent reporters allow detection of metastatic colonies in pre-clinical models (Aiello et al., 2016; Fluegen et al., 2017), an inability to recover pure micron-scale colonies has precluded systematic phenotypic analysis of early-stage metastases.
evidence: This reflects the methodological gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection is the most widely used platform for isolating cells from specific compartments in vivo.
source: Several methods have been developed to isolate cells from specific compartments in vivo, laser-capture microdissection representing the most widely used platform (Basnet et al., 2019; Espina et al., 2006; Lovatt et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies using laser-capture microdissection.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection has limitations including contamination by undesired cells within the capture field.
source: However, the use of these methods is restricted to compartments of particular size and only for specific applications due to several limitations, including (1) contamination by undesired cells within the capture field; (2) low throughput; (3) a need for expensive and temperamental hardware; (4) loss of cell viability; and (5) lack of control over population composition.
evidence: This reflects known limitations of laser-capture microdissection based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection has low throughput.
source: However, the use of these methods is restricted to compartments of particular size and only for specific applications due to several limitations, including (1) contamination by undesired cells within the capture field; (2) low throughput; (3) a need for expensive and temperamental hardware; (4) loss of cell viability; and (5) lack of control over population composition.
evidence: This reflects known limitations of laser-capture microdissection.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection requires expensive and temperamental hardware.
source: However, the use of these methods is restricted to compartments of particular size and only for specific applications due to several limitations, including (1) contamination by undesired cells within the capture field; (2) low throughput; (3) a need for expensive and temperamental hardware; (4) loss of cell viability; and (5) lack of control over population composition.
evidence: This reflects known limitations of laser-capture microdissection.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection results in loss of cell viability.
source: However, the use of these methods is restricted to compartments of particular size and only for specific applications due to several limitations, including (1) contamination by undesired cells within the capture field; (2) low throughput; (3) a need for expensive and temperamental hardware; (4) loss of cell viability; and (5) lack of control over population composition.
evidence: This reflects known limitations of laser-capture microdissection.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection lacks control over population composition.
source: However, the use of these methods is restricted to compartments of particular size and only for specific applications due to several limitations, including (1) contamination by undesired cells within the capture field; (2) low throughput; (3) a need for expensive and temperamental hardware; (4) loss of cell viability; and (5) lack of control over population composition.
evidence: This reflects known limitations of laser-capture microdissection.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics methods can distinguish local patterns across large tumor regions.
source: Spatial transcriptomics methods continue to improve and can distinguish local patterns across large tumor regions (Moncada et al., 2020), but resolution limits and low representation of small metastatic colonies in the tissue hinders their isolation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on spatial transcriptomics.

claim: Resolution limits and low representation of small metastatic colonies in tissue hinders isolation by spatial transcriptomics methods.
source: Spatial transcriptomics methods continue to improve and can distinguish local patterns across large tumor regions (Moncada et al., 2020), but resolution limits and low representation of small metastatic colonies in the tissue hinders their isolation.
evidence: This reflects current limitations of spatial transcriptomics technology.

claim: Photoactivable and photoconvertible proteins provide a promising alternative for targeted cell isolation.
source: Photoactivable and photoconvertible proteins provide a promising alternative for targeted cell isolation (Medaglia et al., 2017; Nicenboim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using photoconvertible proteins.

claim: Existing photoconversion systems require specialized equipment and extended handling times.
source: However, existing systems require specialized equipment and extended handling times, thus limiting scalability and precluding effective acquisition of rare or sporadic cells from multiple compartments such as microcolonies.
evidence: This reflects limitations of existing photoconversion-based methods.

claim: Existing photoconversion systems limit scalability and preclude effective acquisition of rare or sporadic cells from multiple compartments.
source: However, existing systems require specialized equipment and extended handling times, thus limiting scalability and precluding effective acquisition of rare or sporadic cells from multiple compartments such as microcolonies.
evidence: This reflects limitations of existing photoconversion-based methods.

claim: Exposure of H2B-Dendra2-expressing pancreatic tumor cells to mercury lamp-generated violet light for 30 seconds efficiently marks all cells within the field of view.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, exposure of H2B–Dendra2-expressing pancreatic tumor cells (5074 cell line) to a mercury lamp-generated violet light (400–450 nm) for 30 s efficiently marks all cells within the field of view (FOV).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Orthotopic injection of 10^4 6419c5-H2B-Dendra2 cells into the pancreas of C57BL/6 mice generates metastases after 3-5 weeks.
source: To generate metastasis, 104 6419c5–H2B–Dendra2 cells were injected into the pancreas of immune competent C57BL/6 mice, and tumors were allowed to grow for 3–5 weeks, at which point livers were examined under a standard widefield microscope.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used to generate the model.

claim: Metastatic foci in the liver range from solitary tumor cells to micrometastases and larger macrometastases.
source: Imaging revealed metastatic foci of various sizes, ranging from solitary tumor cells to micrometastases and larger macrometastases (Figure 1B, left).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Strong nuclear fluorescence in all tumor cells enables easy detection of metastatic foci with a low magnification 4× objective.
source: Importantly, strong nuclear fluorescence in all tumor cells enabled easy detection of metastatic foci of a particular size even with a low magnification 4× objective, allowing for rapid identification of regions of interest.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data and experimental observations.

claim: Exposure to 400-450 nm light for less than 5 seconds using a 40× objective leads to robust induction of red fluorescence in all cancer cells within the boundaries of the limited FOV.
source: Exposure for <5 s (40× objective, N.A. = 0.75) led to a robust induction of red fluorescence in all cancer cells within the boundaries of the limited FOV (Figure 1B, 'Postconversion').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hundreds of cancer cells within a macrometastasis can be rapidly photoconverted in 15 seconds using a 10× objective.
source: In a different FOV, using a 10× objective, we rapidly photoconverted (15 s, N.A. = 0.4) hundreds of cancer cells within a macrometastasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Spatial precision of photoconversion labeling is achieved even when a low magnification objective is used, with a rapid drop-off of photoconversion outside the FOV boundary.
source: Spatial precision of labeling was achieved even when a low magnification objective was used, with a rapid drop-off of photoconversion outside the FOV boundary (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Background red fluorescence in non-converted Dendra2-H2B+ cells is low, indicating minimal spontaneous conversion.
source: Importantly, background red fluorescence in non-converted Dendra2–H2B+ cells was low, indicating minimal spontaneous conversion in our experimental model (Figure 1B,D, top left).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Photoconverted cells derived from microcolonies and macrometastases show strong, comparable increases (~30-fold) in red fluorescence intensity.
source: Following flow sorting, photoconverted cells derived from the different groups showed strong, comparable increases (~30-fold) in red fluorescence intensity (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Red fluorescence increases with longer exposure times, but 5 seconds is sufficient to permit detection of photoconverted cells.
source: Although red fluorescence increased with longer exposure times, 5 s was sufficient to permit detection of photoconverted cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Recovery of photoconverted microcolonies averaged at 38% across 16 isolation sessions.
source: Across these sessions, recovery of photoconverted microcolonies (Dendra-red+ cells detected by flow cytometry as a % of total photoconverted cells quantified by microscopy) averaged at 38% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: A moderate output of 80-170 cells can be acquired per hour using the PIC-IT experimental setup.
source: Thus, a moderate output of 80–170 cells can be acquired per hour using this experimental setup (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: There is minimal decay in the red signal up to 7 hours post-photoconversion.
source: Notably, we typically used less than 30% of the liver in our marking sessions; consequently, cell yield could potentially be improved with longer sessions, as there was minimal decay in the red signal up to 7 hr post-photoconversion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Cells remain viable after flow sorting, with a ~70% seeding efficiency measured 24 hours after plating.
source: Cells remained viable after flow sorting, with a ~70% seeding efficiency measured 24 hr after plating (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cells sorted following photoconversion show no evidence of DNA damage.
source: Importantly, cells sorted following photoconversion showed no evidence of DNA damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) or impairment of colony formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by γ-H2AX staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Cells sorted following photoconversion show no impairment of colony formation.
source: Importantly, cells sorted following photoconversion showed no evidence of DNA damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) or impairment of colony formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 361 metastatic and primary tumor cells revealed expression of dendra2 and Krt19 but not markers of hepatocytes, endothelial cells, immune cells, and fibroblasts.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 361 metastatic and primary tumor cells via Cel-seq2 (Hashimshony et al., 2016) revealed expression of dendra2 and Krt19 but not markers of hepatocytes, endothelial cells, immune cells, and fibroblasts (Figure 1F), confirming the purity of the isolated cell populations.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The RNA-seq expression analysis confirms the purity of the isolated cell populations.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 361 metastatic and primary tumor cells via Cel-seq2 (Hashimshony et al., 2016) revealed expression of dendra2 and Krt19 but not markers of hepatocytes, endothelial cells, immune cells, and fibroblasts (Figure 1F), confirming the purity of the isolated cell populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of contaminating cell markers in the RNA-seq data.

claim: Clca3a1 expression is significantly higher in macrometastases than microcolonies.
source: To further validate this RNA-seq expression analysis, we identified two genes – Clca3a1 and Bnip3 – whose expression was predicted to be significantly higher in macrometastases than microcolonies.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G and flow cytometry data in Figure 1H.

claim: Bnip3 expression is significantly higher in macrometastases than microcolonies.
source: To further validate this RNA-seq expression analysis, we identified two genes – Clca3a1 and Bnip3 – whose expression was predicted to be significantly higher in macrometastases than microcolonies.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I and immunostaining data in Figure 1J.

claim: The difference in Clca3a1 expression between macrometastases and microcolonies was confirmed by flow cytometry.
source: We then confirmed this difference in expression by flow cytometry and immunostaining (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The difference in Bnip3 expression between macrometastases and microcolonies was confirmed by immunostaining.
source: We then confirmed this difference in expression by flow cytometry and immunostaining (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: At a global level, the distribution of microcolony- and macrometastatic-transcriptomes broadly overlapped.
source: At a global level, the distribution of microcolony- and macrometastatic-transcriptomes broadly overlapped (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by UMAP visualization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: UMAP identified three clusters in microcolonies and macrometastases, annotated as proliferative, inflammatory, or hypoxic/stressed.
source: UMAP further identified three clusters in microcolonies and macrometastases, annotated as proliferative, inflammatory, or hypoxic/stressed, suggesting that microcolonies are phenotypically diverse (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by UMAP clustering analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Microcolonies are phenotypically diverse.
source: UMAP further identified three clusters in microcolonies and macrometastases, annotated as proliferative, inflammatory, or hypoxic/stressed, suggesting that microcolonies are phenotypically diverse (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of multiple distinct clusters within microcolonies.

claim: The inflammatory cluster is enriched in microcolonies compared to macrometastases (30% vs. 16%).
source: Notably, the inflammatory cluster, defined by elevated IFN-γ response and complement activity (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), was enriched in microcolonies compared to macrometastases (30% vs. 16%).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The inflammatory cluster is defined by elevated IFN-γ response and complement activity.
source: Notably, the inflammatory cluster, defined by elevated IFN-γ response and complement activity (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), was enriched in microcolonies compared to macrometastases (30% vs. 16%).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both the inflammatory and hypoxic clusters display decreased abundance of proliferation-related transcripts including CCNA2, TOP2A, CDK1, Ki-67, and PCNA.
source: In contrast, both the inflammatory and hypoxic clusters displayed decreased abundance of proliferation-related transcripts including CCNA2, TOP2A, CDK1, Ki-67, and PCNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with previous observations on growth arrest mediated by hypoxia in colonizing metastatic cells (Fluegen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by transcript abundance data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The decreased abundance of proliferation-related transcripts in inflammatory and hypoxic clusters is consistent with previous observations on growth arrest mediated by hypoxia in colonizing metastatic cells.
source: In contrast, both the inflammatory and hypoxic clusters displayed decreased abundance of proliferation-related transcripts including CCNA2, TOP2A, CDK1, Ki-67, and PCNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with previous observations on growth arrest mediated by hypoxia in colonizing metastatic cells (Fluegen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and comparison with current data.

claim: Differential gene analysis revealed 500 genes that were more highly expressed in microcolonies and 366 genes that were more highly expressed in macrometastases.
source: Next, we conducted a differential gene analysis using EdgeR (Robinson et al., 2010), comparing the transcriptomes of 94 microcolonies to 111 macrometastatic cells. This revealed 500 genes that were more highly expressed in microcolonies and 366 genes that were more highly expressed in macrometastases (p<0.05, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Functional annotation of microcolony-associated genes revealed a strong signal for TNF-α-related NF-κB signaling.
source: Functional annotation of the microcolony-associated genes revealed a strong signal for TNF-α-related NF-κB signaling and a prominent increase in inflammatory cytokine secretion (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Functional annotation of microcolony-associated genes revealed a prominent increase in inflammatory cytokine secretion.
source: Functional annotation of the microcolony-associated genes revealed a strong signal for TNF-α-related NF-κB signaling and a prominent increase in inflammatory cytokine secretion (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: An IFN-γ-response signature is enriched in microcolonies.
source: Likewise, an IFN-γ-response signature was enriched in microcolonies, consistent with a pattern of enriched inflammatory gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the functional annotation analysis.

claim: Transcription factor motif analysis revealed enrichment of pro-inflammatory DNA regulatory elements in microcolonies.
source: Furthermore, transcription factor motif analysis (HOMER) revealed enrichment of pro-inflammatory DNA regulatory elements in microcolonies (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by HOMER motif analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Motif analysis revealed enrichment of binding sites for NF-κB, JUN/AP-1, and STAT in microcolonies.
source: In addition to the known inflammation-related transcription factors NF-κB, JUN/AP-1, and STAT, motif analysis also revealed enrichment of binding sites for MAFK, which has recently been demonstrated to enhance the transcriptional response to NF-κB (Hwang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by HOMER motif analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Motif analysis revealed enrichment of binding sites for MAFK in microcolonies.
source: In addition to the known inflammation-related transcription factors NF-κB, JUN/AP-1, and STAT, motif analysis also revealed enrichment of binding sites for MAFK, which has recently been demonstrated to enhance the transcriptional response to NF-κB (Hwang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by HOMER motif analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MAFK has been demonstrated to enhance the transcriptional response to NF-κB.
source: In addition to the known inflammation-related transcription factors NF-κB, JUN/AP-1, and STAT, motif analysis also revealed enrichment of binding sites for MAFK, which has recently been demonstrated to enhance the transcriptional response to NF-κB (Hwang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 29 genes associated with the Hallmark 'TNF-α-signaling-via-NF-κB' gene set were expressed at significantly higher levels in microcolonies compared to macrometastatic cells.
source: In line with this enrichment of TNF-related NF-κB signaling, 29 genes associated with the Hallmark 'TNF-α-signaling-via-NF-κB' gene set were expressed at significantly higher levels in microcolonies compared to macrometastastic cells (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Transcriptional profiling suggests that pancreatic microcolonies in the liver manifest a strong pro-inflammatory phenotype associated with increase in NF-κB and AP-1 signaling.
source: Taken together, transcriptional profiling suggests that pancreatic microcolonies in the liver manifest a strong pro-inflammatory phenotype associated with increase in NF-κB and AP-1 signaling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence from RNA-seq, motif analysis, and functional annotation.

claim: Functional annotation indicated enrichment for cell cycle and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways in macrometastases.
source: We next turned our attention to the genes with low expression in microcolonies relative to macrometastases. Intriguingly, functional annotation indicated enrichment for cell cycle and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways in the macrometastases (Figure 3A), with elevated expression of a number of mitosis regulators such as Nek2 (Fry et al., 2012), Sapcd2 (Xu et al., 2007), and Ttk (Dominguez-Brauer et al., 2015, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Macrometastases show elevated expression of mitosis regulators such as Nek2, Sapcd2, and Ttk.
source: We next turned our attention to the genes with low expression in microcolonies relative to macrometastases. Intriguingly, functional annotation indicated enrichment for cell cycle and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways in the macrometastases (Figure 3A), with elevated expression of a number of mitosis regulators such as Nek2 (Fry et al., 2012), Sapcd2 (Xu et al., 2007), and Ttk (Dominguez-Brauer et al., 2015, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B and citations to studies characterizing these genes.

claim: Microcolonies exhibit higher expression of negative regulators of cell cycle progression including Ceacam1, Stard13, and Mir22hg.
source: Consistent with this, microcolonies exhibited higher expression of negative regulators of cell cycle progression including Ceacam1 (Sappino et al., 2012), Stard13 (Jaafar et al., 2020), and Mir22hg (Xu et al., 2020, Figure 3B), predicting an overall hypo-proliferative state for microcolonies.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B and citations to studies characterizing these genes.

claim: The gene expression pattern predicts an overall hypo-proliferative state for microcolonies.
source: Consistent with this, microcolonies exhibited higher expression of negative regulators of cell cycle progression including Ceacam1 (Sappino et al., 2012), Stard13 (Jaafar et al., 2020), and Mir22hg (Xu et al., 2020, Figure 3B), predicting an overall hypo-proliferative state for microcolonies.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns observed.

claim: Ki-67 immunostaining revealed no measurable difference in the percentage of positive cells in microcolonies vs. macrometastases.
source: To determine the proliferative state of the cells, we profiled microcolonies and macrometastases for expression of cell cycle markers by immunofluorescence. Ki-67 immunostaining revealed no measurable difference in the percentage of positive cells in microcolonies vs. macrometastases (Figure 3C), consistent with our previously reported findings (Aiello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The finding of no difference in Ki-67 staining between microcolonies and macrometastases is consistent with previously reported findings.
source: To determine the proliferative state of the cells, we profiled microcolonies and macrometastases for expression of cell cycle markers by immunofluorescence. Ki-67 immunostaining revealed no measurable difference in the percentage of positive cells in microcolonies vs. macrometastases (Figure 3C), consistent with our previously reported findings (Aiello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The frequency of phosphorylated-histone H3-positive cells is lower in microcolonies than macrometastases.
source: However, the frequency of phosphorylated-histone H3-positive cells was lower in microcolonies (Figure 3D), suggesting fewer mitotic events.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Lower frequency of phosphorylated-histone H3-positive cells in microcolonies suggests fewer mitotic events.
source: However, the frequency of phosphorylated-histone H3-positive cells was lower in microcolonies (Figure 3D), suggesting fewer mitotic events.
evidence: This is inferred from the phospho-histone H3 staining data.

claim: The frequency of pRB-positive cells is comparable across metastatic stages.
source: Examination of cell cycle suppressors indicated comparable frequencies of pRB-positive cells across metastatic stages (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Expression levels of pRB are consistently higher in macrometastatic cells than in microcolonies.
source: However, expression levels of pRB were consistently higher in macrometastatic cells, indicating higher propensity for cell cycle progression in these cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Higher pRB expression levels in macrometastatic cells indicate higher propensity for cell cycle progression.
source: However, expression levels of pRB were consistently higher in macrometastatic cells, indicating higher propensity for cell cycle progression in these cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the pRB staining data and knowledge of pRB's role in cell cycle regulation.

claim: There is a trend toward higher prevalence of p21 in microcolonies.
source: Additional staining revealed a trend toward higher prevalence of p21 in microcolonies (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The cycling fractions are similar in microcolonies and macrometastatic cells, but rate of transit through the cell cycle may be slower in microcolonies.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the cycling fractions are similar in microcolonies in macrometastatic cells, but rate of transit through the cell cycle may be slower in microcolonies.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of Ki-67, phospho-histone H3, and pRB staining data.

claim: Cells derived from microcolonies and macrometastases expanded to a similar extent after 24 hours in culture.
source: While cells derived from microcolonies and macrometastases expanded to a similar extent after 24 hr, colonies derived from macrometastases were larger at 48 hr and 72 hr (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3J and 3K.

claim: Colonies derived from macrometastases were larger than those from microcolonies at 48 hours and 72 hours in culture.
source: While cells derived from microcolonies and macrometastases expanded to a similar extent after 24 hr, colonies derived from macrometastases were larger at 48 hr and 72 hr (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3J and 3K.

claim: The ex vivo proliferation results support the molecular profiling results and suggest that macrometastatic cells are primed for cell division.
source: These results support our molecular profiling results and suggest that macrometastatic cells are primed for cell division (or, conversely, that microcolonies are primed for cell cycle arrest).
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of molecular profiling and functional proliferation data.

claim: Microcolonies are primed for cell cycle arrest.
source: These results support our molecular profiling results and suggest that macrometastatic cells are primed for cell division (or, conversely, that microcolonies are primed for cell cycle arrest).
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of molecular profiling and functional proliferation data.

claim: Solitary pancreatic tumor cells exhibit resistance to standard-of-care chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel) in autochthonous KPCY mice.
source: We previously reported that solitary pancreatic tumor cells exhibit resistance to standard-of-care chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel) in autochthonous KPCY mice (Aiello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Microcolonies in the 6419c5 implanted cell line model exhibit higher levels of nuclear NF-κB-p65 compared to macrometastases.
source: First, we performed NF-κB-p65 staining in the 6419 c5 implanted cell line model and the KPCY autochthonous model. These two models confirmed that microcolonies exhibit higher levels of nuclear NF-κB-p65 compared to macrometastases (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Microcolonies in the KPCY autochthonous model exhibit higher levels of nuclear NF-κB-p65 compared to macrometastases.
source: First, we performed NF-κB-p65 staining in the 6419 c5 implanted cell line model and the KPCY autochthonous model. These two models confirmed that microcolonies exhibit higher levels of nuclear NF-κB-p65 compared to macrometastases (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Phospho-c-Jun-positive cells are more prevalent in microcolonies than in macrometastases in both the 6419c5 and KPCY models.
source: In addition, and as suggested from our motif analysis, phospho-c-Jun-positive cells were more prevalent in microcolonies than in macrometastases in both models (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Expression of NF-κB-p65 is enhanced in microcolonies of KPCY mice lacking overt metastatic disease.
source: Expression of NF-κB-p65, and to a lesser degree phospho-c-Jun, was also enhanced in microcolonies of KPCY mice lacking overt metastatic disease (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), suggesting that the pro-inflammatory phenotype does not depend on the presence of large metastases.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Phospho-c-Jun expression is enhanced to a lesser degree in microcolonies of KPCY mice lacking overt metastatic disease.
source: Expression of NF-κB-p65, and to a lesser degree phospho-c-Jun, was also enhanced in microcolonies of KPCY mice lacking overt metastatic disease (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), suggesting that the pro-inflammatory phenotype does not depend on the presence of large metastases.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: The pro-inflammatory phenotype in microcolonies does not depend on the presence of large metastases.
source: Expression of NF-κB-p65, and to a lesser degree phospho-c-Jun, was also enhanced in microcolonies of KPCY mice lacking overt metastatic disease (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), suggesting that the pro-inflammatory phenotype does not depend on the presence of large metastases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that microcolonies show enhanced NF-κB-p65 even in the absence of macrometastases.

claim: The enhanced inflammatory signatures identified through PIC-IT-enabled RNA sequencing reflect true signaling differences in small and large metastases.
source: These findings suggest that the enhanced inflammatory signatures identified through PIC-IT-enabled RNA sequencing reflect true signaling differences in small and large metastases.
evidence: This is inferred from the concordance between RNA-seq data and protein-level validation by immunostaining.

claim: Triptolide is a potent anti-inflammatory agent that inhibits both NF-κB and AP-1 pathways.
source: To functionally test whether this pro-inflammatory response is required for microcolony viability, we tested the activity of triptolide (TPL), a potent anti-inflammatory agent that inhibits both pathways (Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing triptolide's mechanism of action.

claim: The total liver area occupied by metastases was similar in triptolide-treated and vehicle-treated groups.
source: Although the total liver area occupied by metastases (dominated by macrometastases) was similar in the two treatment groups (Figure 4D), triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the relative frequency of microcolonies (Figure 4E) and the ratio of microcolonies or single-metastatic cells to macrometastases (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the relative frequency of microcolonies.
source: Although the total liver area occupied by metastases (dominated by macrometastases) was similar in the two treatment groups (Figure 4D), triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the relative frequency of microcolonies (Figure 4E) and the ratio of microcolonies or single-metastatic cells to macrometastases (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the ratio of microcolonies to macrometastases.
source: Although the total liver area occupied by metastases (dominated by macrometastases) was similar in the two treatment groups (Figure 4D), triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the relative frequency of microcolonies (Figure 4E) and the ratio of microcolonies or single-metastatic cells to macrometastases (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the ratio of single-metastatic cells to macrometastases.
source: Although the total liver area occupied by metastases (dominated by macrometastases) was similar in the two treatment groups (Figure 4D), triptolide treatment led to a significant reduction in the relative frequency of microcolonies (Figure 4E) and the ratio of microcolonies or single-metastatic cells to macrometastases (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The triptolide results are in line with a recent report highlighting the potential of neoadjuvant treatment with NF-kB-targeting therapy in PDAC.
source: These results are in line with a recent report highlighting the potential of neoadjuvant treatment with NF-kB-targeting therapy in PDAC (Saito et al., 2019) and suggest that microcolonies are more susceptible to inhibition of inflammatory signaling than macrometastases.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Microcolonies are more susceptible to inhibition of inflammatory signaling than macrometastases.
source: These results are in line with a recent report highlighting the potential of neoadjuvant treatment with NF-kB-targeting therapy in PDAC (Saito et al., 2019) and suggest that microcolonies are more susceptible to inhibition of inflammatory signaling than macrometastases.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential response to triptolide treatment.

claim: PIC-IT permits the isolation and systematic characterization of cells comprising both large and small metastatic lesions.
source: Studying the occult fraction of metastatic disease is challenging due to the rarity of cells comprising micrometastatic lesions and a lack of efficient tools to isolate and study them. PIC-IT overcomes these challenges and permits the isolation and systematic characterization of cells comprising both large and small metastatic lesions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data demonstrating the technique's capabilities throughout the manuscript.

claim: Microcolonies are a diverse cell population enriched with cells manifesting a pro-inflammatory response.
source: Our experiments reveal that microcolonies are a diverse cell population enriched with cells manifesting a pro-inflammatory response.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis and gene expression data.

claim: NF-κB/AP-1-regulated inflammatory pathways play a specific role in microcolonies not shared by the majority of metastatic cells (macrometastases).
source: Our findings further highlight a specific role for NF-κB/AP-1-regulated inflammatory pathways in microcolonies not shared by the majority of metastatic cells (macrometastases), demonstrating the utility of our approach in identifying susceptibilities of a micro-fraction of the metastatic population that drives disease recurrence and mortality.
evidence: This is supported by the differential response to NF-κB inhibition and the gene expression data.

claim: Inflammation plays a key role in tumor initiation and progression in PDAC.
source: Inflammation plays a key role in tumor initiation and progression in PDAC and has also been implicated in metastasis formation (Stone and Beatty, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Inflammation has been implicated in metastasis formation in PDAC.
source: Inflammation plays a key role in tumor initiation and progression in PDAC and has also been implicated in metastasis formation (Stone and Beatty, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Non-uniform NF-kB signaling across the metastatic spectrum could potentially reflect altered levels of TNF-α in the microenvironment of a growing metastasis.
source: Non-uniform NF-kB signaling across the metastatic spectrum in our study is somewhat surprising and could potentially reflect altered levels of TNF-α in the microenvironment of a growing metastasis (Milette et al., 2017) or a pre-existing 'NF-kB' activity associated with tumor dissemination.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to a relevant study.

claim: Non-uniform NF-kB signaling across the metastatic spectrum could potentially reflect a pre-existing 'NF-kB' activity associated with tumor dissemination.
source: Non-uniform NF-kB signaling across the metastatic spectrum in our study is somewhat surprising and could potentially reflect altered levels of TNF-α in the microenvironment of a growing metastasis (Milette et al., 2017) or a pre-existing 'NF-kB' activity associated with tumor dissemination.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Marked upregulation of TNF-α-NF-kB signaling has been observed in PDAC CTCs.
source: Of note, this latter possibility is hinted at by marked upregulation of TNF-α-NF-kB signaling in PDAC CTCs (Ting et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on circulating tumor cells.

claim: It remains to be determined whether the pro-inflammatory profile in microcolonies reflects the pre-metastatic state of the 'seed' or an acquired adaptation to the 'soil'.
source: Nonetheless, as isolated microcolonies may originate in either primary tumor or metastasis, it remains to be determined whether the pro-inflammatory profile reflects the pre-metastatic state of the 'seed' or an acquired adaptation to the 'soil'.
evidence: This acknowledges an unresolved question about the origin of the observed phenotype.

claim: TNF-α-mediated NF-kB signaling can specifically attenuate cell cycle transition through the G1/S boundary.
source: Although the mechanism underlying reduced pRB phosphorylation and hypo-proliferative state in microcolonies is unclear, a recent study demonstrated that TNF-α-mediated NF-kB signaling can specifically attenuate cell cycle transition through the G1/S boundary (Ankers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on NF-kB signaling and cell cycle regulation.

claim: PIC-IT could be used to isolate cells in different 'niches' of the tumor microenvironment.
source: While the current study used PIC-IT to isolate cells at different stages of metastasis, the method has many potential applications. For example, it could be used to isolate cells in different 'niches' of the tumor microenvironment (e.g. cells in well perfused vs. poorly perfused regions), thus paving the way for testing functional features such as proliferation, migration, metabolic characteristics, and drug resistance in heterogeneous tumor cell populations.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the technique.

claim: PIC-IT could enable testing functional features such as proliferation, migration, metabolic characteristics, and drug resistance in heterogeneous tumor cell populations.
source: While the current study used PIC-IT to isolate cells at different stages of metastasis, the method has many potential applications. For example, it could be used to isolate cells in different 'niches' of the tumor microenvironment (e.g. cells in well perfused vs. poorly perfused regions), thus paving the way for testing functional features such as proliferation, migration, metabolic characteristics, and drug resistance in heterogeneous tumor cell populations.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the technique.

claim: PIC-IT can be used to identify protein markers with which to prospectively isolate cells of interest by flow cytometry.
source: As our identification of CLCA1 shows, the technique can be used to identify protein markers – particularly those residing on the cell surface – with which to prospectively isolate cells of interest by flow cytometry.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental demonstration of CLCA1 as a marker differentially expressed between microcolonies and macrometastases.

claim: PIC-IT is particularly well suited to the isolation of spatially defined rare cells such as stem cells in malignant and benign conditions.
source: Finally, the technique is particularly well suited to the isolation of spatially defined rare cells – such as stem cells – in malignant and benign conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the technique.

claim: The majority of microcolonies collected were 1-2 cells in size.
source: Microcolonies were defined as collections of 10 or fewer metastatic cells, with the majority being one or two cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), while macrometastases were defined as lesions of >400 µm in diameter.
evidence: This is supported by the size distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Macrometastases were defined as lesions of >400 µm in diameter.
source: Microcolonies were defined as collections of 10 or fewer metastatic cells, with the majority being one or two cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), while macrometastases were defined as lesions of >400 µm in diameter.
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Over 95% of mice develop macrometastases by 21 days after orthotopic implantation of 6419c5-YFP cells.
source: We inoculated 6419c5-YFP cells into the pancreas and allowed implants to grow for 21 days (Figure 4C), a time point at which >95% of mice develop macrometastases (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental model, though the data is not shown.
